name: Sarah M - Apr 28
transcript:
Therapist: Good morning Sarah, how have you been since our last session?

Sarah: Hi. It's been a rough week honestly. The anxiety has been really bad, especially in the mornings. I wake up with this tightness in my chest and my mind just starts racing about everything I need to do.

Therapist: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me more about what the racing thoughts focus on?

Sarah: It's mostly work stuff. I have this big presentation coming up next week and I keep imagining all the ways it could go wrong. Like, what if I forget what I'm supposed to say? What if people think I'm incompetent? I know rationally that I'm good at my job but the feelings just take over.

Therapist: That sounds like the anticipatory anxiety pattern we've discussed before. Have you been able to use any of the grounding techniques we practiced?

Sarah: I tried the 5-4-3-2-1 thing a couple of times. It helps in the moment but then twenty minutes later the anxiety comes back. I feel like I'm just putting a bandaid on it.

Therapist: It's actually very normal for grounding to provide temporary relief rather than permanent resolution. The goal isn't to eliminate anxiety entirely but to build your capacity to move through it. Have you noticed any patterns in when the anxiety spikes versus when it's more manageable?

Sarah: Yeah, actually. It's worse when I'm alone, like in the morning before my roommate wakes up, or late at night. When I'm busy or with people it's better. But I can't be busy every second of the day.

Therapist: That's a really insightful observation. The isolation amplifies the anxious thoughts because there's nothing else competing for your attention. Let's talk about building a morning routine that gives your mind something structured to engage with before the anxiety has a chance to escalate.

Sarah: That would be helpful. I've been meaning to start meditating but I can never stick with it.

Therapist: Let's not put pressure on meditation specifically. What's something you genuinely enjoy that you could do for ten minutes each morning?

Sarah: I like drawing. I used to sketch every day in college but I stopped when I got my job.

Therapist: That could be perfect. Creative activities engage a different part of the brain than the analytical rumination cycle. Would you be willing to try ten minutes of sketching each morning this week as an experiment?

Sarah: Yeah, I think I could do that. It doesn't feel as intimidating as meditation.

Therapist: Great. And I want to revisit the presentation anxiety. You mentioned knowing rationally that you're competent but the feelings override that. Can we look at some evidence from your actual track record?

Sarah: I mean, I've given presentations before and they've gone fine. My manager even said my last quarterly review presentation was one of the best on the team.

Therapist: So we have concrete evidence that contradicts the catastrophic predictions. I'd like you to write down three specific times you've succeeded at something you were anxious about. Keep that list somewhere you can see it when the anxiety spikes. Not as a way to argue with the feelings, but as a reminder that your anxiety's predictions have been wrong before.

Sarah: Okay. I can do that. Thank you, I feel a bit better just talking about it.

Therapist: That's what this space is for. Before we wrap up, how are things going with sleep? Last time you mentioned having trouble falling asleep.

Sarah: It's a little better actually. I've been putting my phone in another room at night like you suggested and I think I'm falling asleep about 30 minutes faster. Still waking up early though.

Therapist: That's progress. The early waking often correlates with the morning anxiety. As we address one, the other tends to improve too. Let's plan to check in on both next week. Same time?

Sarah: Yes, same time works. Thanks.
